previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes, bilateral below-knee amputations, and a history of recurrent resistant urinary tract infections was admitted with urosepsis and bacteremia. She presented with dysuria and hypotension, and urine cultures grew ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae and Citrobacter freundii, while blood cultures grew Enterococcus faecalis. She also had Candida glabrata in her urine, prompting antifungal treatment. Imaging showed colitis-like changes without symptoms and no evidence of a rectovaginal fistula despite stool found in the vaginal vault. She experienced a transient drop in hemoglobin requiring transfusion and had a brief episode of asymptomatic ventricular tachycardia. Her home metoprolol and lisinopril were held during hypotension and restarted when her blood pressure stabilized. Insulin and gabapentin were adjusted. She improved with meropenem, vancomycin, tigecycline, and fluconazole, and was transitioned to ertapenem via PICC line for outpatient completion of therapy. She was discharged home with nursing services, stable and alert, on a regimen including oral vancomycin, fluconazole, and IV ertapenem, with follow-up planned in multiple specialties.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ woman with history of diabetes mellitus type I, PVD 
s/p bilateral BKA with multiple revisions, wound infections, 
ESBL Klebsiella urosepsis (pan-resistant), C dif colitis, and 
recent admission for bacteremia urosepsis. She presents today 
due to abnormal labs (elevated transaminases) drawn as 
outpatient on the day prior to admission.

The transaminitis was felt to be secondary to the antibiotics 
she had recently received. Both fluconazole and ertepenam can 
cause elevations in transaminases. In addition, patient was 
taking her regular statin dose, which could have contributed. 
All of these medicines were stopped (her fluconazole and 
ertepenam course, in fact, she had completed on the day prior to 
admission). She never had abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, 
diarrhea, or anorexia. Her abdominal exam was normal. Given that 
the transaminases were downtrending on the second hospital day, 
RUQ ultrasound was not felt to be warranted. She will have liver 
enzymes drawn on ___ of this week and faxed to her primary 
care physician.

With repect to her other issues:

# Acute renal failure: resolved with intravenous fluids. Urine 
culture is pending at time of discharge.

# Hyperkalemia, without electrocardiographic changes: resolved 
with kayexalate in the emergency ward and intravenous fluids 
overnight on the medical floor.

# Anemia: hematocrit was stable and at baseline. Previous iron 
studies have been suggestive of an anemia of chronic disease.

# Hypertension: no active concerns. Her home blood pressure 
medicines were continued.

# Diabetes: no active concerns. Her home insulin regimen was 
continued.

# Recent urinary tract infection, urosepsis, and bacteremia: 
patient was recently admitted for klebsiella and citrobacter 
urinary tract infection, as well as enterococcal bacteremia. She 
was treated with ertepenam and vancomycin (14+days) as well as 
fluconazole for candidal urinary tract infection. All of these 
antibiotics were completed yesterday. She continues on oral 
vancomycin until ___ for C dif infection.

# Stool in vaginal vault: this was noted during her previous 
admission. Gynecology, colorectal surgery, and urology services 
were all consulted. Patient had 2 CT ___ with rectal 
contrast, both of which were negative for obvious fistula. 
Colorectal surgery did not see obvious fistula and thus, there 
was no need for surgery. Fistula was not appreciated on gyn 
exam, however stool was seen in vaginal vault. Patient has an 
outpatient appointment in colorectal surgery clinic for 
continued investigation.
